question: How should large Transformers be partitioned across chips to serve generative inference at tight latency and long context efficiently?
hypothesis: An analytical model of communication cost can pick the best multi-axis partitioning per workload (batch, context, latency target), and multiquery attention sharded over batch removes the KV-cache bottleneck.
contributions: Analytical model of inference cost used to select partitioning layouts (1D/2D weight-stationary, weight-gathered)
Multiquery attention partitioned over batch, enabling up to 32x longer context
Low-level optimizations (Looped CollectiveEinsum, int8 weights) giving a new Pareto frontier of latency vs MFU vs FasterTransformer
29 ms/token decode and 76% MFU prefill on PaLM 540B

method.summary: Inference framework in JAX/XLA on TPU v4 with an analytical communication-cost model to choose between weight-stationary and weight-gathered feedforward layouts and head- or batch-sharded attention. Evaluated on PaLM 8B/62B/540B and a Megatron-Turing 530B variant, sweeping batch size and chip count, and compared by MFU with FasterTransformer.

limits: No variance or repeated runs; Pareto points are single measurements.
Activation quantization not implemented; int8 large-batch path lacks optimizations, so high-throughput configs use bfloat16.
Hardware is TPU v4 3D torus; GPU generalization is asserted, not measured; FasterTransformer comparison uses different chips and is by MFU only.
FLOPs and communication volume fundamentally limit dense models (conclusion); sparsity/MoE and adaptive compute suggested as future work.
PaLM 540B may be improvable in the high-throughput regime by reducing model parallelism (Appendix C).
No batch sizes below 4 reported for batch-sharded multiquery attention.
